section_title: Why can Paul face suffering without shame?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God. 9 He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began. 10 And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel,

11 to which I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher. 12 For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.

context_lines: Paul asks Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord’s testimony or of Paul as a prisoner. Instead, he is to share in suffering for the gospel through God’s power. Paul grounds that appeal in what God has already done: saved them and called them to a holy life by grace, rather than because of their works.

That grace belongs to God’s purpose before time began and has now been revealed through Christ’s appearing. Christ has defeated death and brought life and immortality into the light through the gospel. The message Paul was appointed to preach is also the reason he suffers.

His confidence rests in the One he has believed. The BSB main text describes Paul entrusting something to God for safekeeping until that day; its footnote also records the reading of something entrusted to Paul. The object is explained differently, but the declaration centers on God’s ability to guard.
common_interpretation_lines: Major Christian traditions agree that God’s grace comes before any claim to have earned salvation. They differ over how His eternal purpose relates to human response. The Reformed [Westminster Confession 3.5–6](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html) teaches an election that does not depend on foreseen faith. [Wesley’s notes on Ephesians 1:4–5](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/) instead describe God’s settled purpose to adopt those whom He foreknows as believing. Both locate salvation in God’s grace and Christ, while explaining that choosing differently.

For verse 12, [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-timothy/) understands the entrusted thing as Paul’s soul, and [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/2_timothy/1.htm) as his eternal life. The [USCCB note](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/2timothy/1) also records the possible reading of the faith entrusted to Paul. These readings emphasize either God keeping Paul’s life and future or God preserving the message committed to him.
god_plan_lines: The passage itself gives the wider story: grace purposed before time, revealed through Christ’s coming, and announced through the gospel. [Ephesians 1:3–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/1.htm) similarly places God’s saving purpose in Christ before the foundation of the world and looks toward all things being brought together in Him.

[1 Corinthians 15:20–26, 50–57](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm) connects Christ’s resurrection with the final defeat of death and the resurrection of His people. Paul’s present chains do not cancel that future. The confidence he commends is grounded in Christ’s victory, rather than a promise that faithful service will avoid suffering.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
